BadGateway.description: A device or backend failed, or the requested capability is not available in this daemon's configuration.

BadRequest.description: The request was malformed, out of range, or refused by the motion guard.

Conflict.description: The device's soft-kill latch is engaged, or a device or mode policy refused an otherwise valid command.

GatewayTimeout.description: A device operation exceeded its deadline. The command may still have taken effect: it is not safe to assume a timeout means nothing happened.

NotFound.description: No such route, or no such navigation goal, trajectory job or expression.

Advisory.description:
One suggestion about one device's current state.

Additive everywhere it appears: absent when the state earns none.

code.description: The stable word to branch on.

message.description: One sentence for a human, naming the state and the next step.

severity.description: How much attention this asks for.

oneOf.description:
The call that changes the state, when the next step IS a call.

Absent when it is not: a lift whose daemon was started without
`[slider] commissioning = true` is moved on by editing that file and
restarting, and there is no verb for that on purpose (the REST
surface is unauthenticated, so a verb that turned commissioning on
would be a verb that turned every other gate off). An advisory with
no action still names the step in `message`.

AdvisoryCode.description:
A stable machine word for one advisory, independent of its wording.

A consumer branches on this, never on [`Advisory::message`] — the same
rule [`crate::ErrorKind`] states for failures, for the same reason.

AdvisorySeverity.description:
How much of an operator's attention one advisory asks for.

An enum rather than a bare string so a later advisory can be published at
a higher severity without any consumer changing the shape it parses.
Today exactly one severity is produced: both the arm's idle state and the
lift's uncommissioned origin are states the machine is legitimately in,
so they are information and nothing more.

ArmBrakeEngageReason.description: Why the brakes were last engaged.

confirm.description:
Must be exactly `RELEASE_BRAKE`. Anything else is a `400`, and the body
is required: the arm drops under gravity the moment the brakes open,
and an empty POST is how a console button or a curl retry reaches a
route by accident.

seconds.description:
How long the brakes stay open before the daemon engages them itself,
in seconds, `1..=120`. Omitted is `30`. Sending the request again while
released restarts the window.

ArmBrakeReport.description: One arm's holding-brake state as this daemon commanded it.

holder.description:
The arm-lease holder that asked for the current release, when the
request named one.

oneOf.description: Why the brakes were last engaged by this daemon, if they ever were.

released.description:
Whether this daemon has forced this arm's holding brakes OPEN and not
closed them since. While `true`, nothing holds the arm but whoever is
supporting it.

The controller acknowledges brake writes but does not report the brake
state back, so this is the daemon's command record, not a sensor.

remaining_s.description:
Seconds left before the daemon re-engages the brakes itself. `None`
while engaged; `0` if the window ran out and the re-engage has not
been confirmed yet (see the daemon log).

window_s.description:
The window the current release was granted, in seconds. `None` while
engaged.

arm.description: Arm section prefix as it appears in `robot.ini` (e.g. `R.A0`).

ArmCheckPoseRequest.description: `POST /v1/arm/check_pose`: a read-only guard query over both arms.

joints_a_deg.description:
Arm A joint angles in degrees; seven values, or empty to check arm B
alone.

joints_b_deg.description:
Arm B joint angles in degrees; seven values, or empty to check arm A
alone.

joints_deg.description: Joint angles in degrees; seven values.

ArmControllerIdentity.description:
Identity of the arm controller board, read from `hostname`, `uname`,
`/etc/os-release`, `uptime`, and `date`.

controller_time.description:
The board's own wall-clock reading from `date`, preserved verbatim
(the board reports it in its own locale).

ArmControllerServos.description:
Board servo/EtherCAT state: masters and their rings, per-joint calibration,
recent faults, and a derived health verdict.

captured_unix_ms.description: Capture time on the firmware host, Unix epoch milliseconds.

masters.description: EtherCAT masters and their slave rings.

recent_faults.description: Recent controller faults scanned from the vendor log tail.

source.description: Where this report came from (e.g. `root@192.168.9.100` or `sim`).

ArmControllerStatus.description:
Board device state: identity, vendor processes, kernel modules, network,
and a derived health verdict.

captured_unix_ms.description: Capture time on the firmware host, Unix epoch milliseconds.

reachable.description: Whether the board answered the diagnostics request.

source.description: Where this report came from (e.g. `root@192.168.9.100` or `sim`).

ArmFeedback.description:
Both arms' narrowed feedback from ONE controller feedback frame.

The arm controller reports both sides in a single datagram at its native
rate (1 kHz on hardware, 100 Hz against the simulator), so this is the
unit an observer receives: one frame, two sides. It exists as a core type
so a consumer that only wants to WATCH the arm — the telemetry sampler —
can do so through the core abstraction without depending on the backend
crate's wider `ArmSnapshot`, which additionally carries wire-level fields
(impedance type, commanded pose, configuration-parameter serials) that
only the backend's own command sequencing needs.

a.description: Arm A, the robot's physical LEFT arm.

b.description: Arm B, the robot's physical RIGHT arm.

ArmLease.description:
The published view of the lease, as `POST /v1/arm/lease`,
`GET /v1/arm/lease` and the `arm.lease` slot of `GET /v1/state` return it.

class.description:
The privilege class the holder claimed. A request of a strictly higher
class takes these arms away; an equal or lower one is refused.

epoch.description:
Monotonic grant counter, incremented on every FRESH grant and left
alone by a heartbeat renewal.

This is what tells a consumer that reads `holder == "me"` whether it
is the same grant it had a moment ago: an unchanged `epoch` means it
never lost the arms, while a higher one means it was displaced and
later granted them again — and therefore that whatever it believed
about the arms' pose, mode or tool registration is stale.

expires_in_s.description:
Whole seconds until the lease expires, rounded up. Once this reaches
zero the lease is gone: the next caller takes it without asking.

holder.description: The self-declared name of the consumer holding the arms.

preempted_from.description:
The holder this lease was taken away from, when it was taken by
preemption rather than granted freely. `null` for an ordinary grant.

It survives renewals, because it describes how this grant came about
and that does not change when the holder heartbeats.

ttl_s.description: The TTL this lease was granted with, in seconds.

holder.description:
The holder releasing the lease. Releasing somebody else's lease is
refused with 409: a release is a consumer yielding, never a takeover.

ArmLeaseRequest.description: `POST /v1/arm/lease`: take, renew, or preempt the arm lease.

oneOf.description:
How privileged this request is: `ambient`, `policy` or `operator`.
**Omitted means `ambient`**, the lowest privilege there is.

That default is the whole reason this could ship without a flag day.
Every consumer that already speaks the lease sends no class, so on the
day the daemon is upgraded all of them rank lowest and nothing they do
changes: no existing caller is silently promoted into a position where
it can take the arms off a person. Privilege is something a consumer
opts into, one release at a time, as it is taught what it is — teleop
and the console claim `operator`, d1-inference claims `policy`, and
omakase-core is correct exactly as it is.

holder.description:
The consumer's own name, echoed back in every refusal so an operator
can see who to ask. Free-form, but use something a human can act on:
`dx-vr-teleop`, `omakaseos`, `console`.

ttl_s.description:
How long the lease should live, in seconds. Omitted means
[`DEFAULT_LEASE_TTL_S`]; the accepted range is `1..=600`. Re-POST with
the same holder to heartbeat.

oneOf.description: The arm is idle.
The arm is in joint-position mode.
The arm is in PVT mode.
The arm is in torque mode.
The arm is released/floating.
The arm controller reports an error.
A controller mode not known by this core version.

unknown.description: A controller mode not known by this core version.

ArmModeCommand.description:
The advertised request body of `POST /v1/arm/{side}/mode`.

This is a *flattened, advertise-only* view of the tagged
[`d1fw_core::ArmModeRequest`] enum with the arm lease's optional `holder`
folded in as a top-level field. The daemon still deserializes the wire
body into `ArmModeRequest` and reads `holder` off it separately (see
`d1fw_front_rest::lease`); nothing deserializes into this struct. It exists
only so the published document describes the body as one flat object.

`openapi-python-client` silently skips any endpoint whose request body is
an `allOf` containing a `oneOf`, which is exactly what the tagged enum plus
a composed-in `holder` used to emit — so `POST /v1/arm/{side}/mode`, the
most-used arm verb, was missing from every generated Python client. A
single flat object with a `mode` string discriminator and every per-variant
parameter optional generates cleanly. Which fields are required for a given
`mode`, and their defaults, are documented on [`d1fw_core::ArmModeRequest`]
and enforced by the daemon, not by this looser schema.

acc_ratio.description:
Acceleration ratio, as a backend-defined normalized ratio
(`0.0..=1.0`). Used by the same four modes as `vel_ratio`.

adjustment_limit_mm.description:
`force_compliance`: how far, in millimetres, the controller may
displace the end effector to comply. Must be positive.

anchor_command_pose.description:
`force_compliance`: write the measured pose into the controller's
commanded pose before the transition. On by default, unsafe to disable.

control_params.description:
`force_compliance`: force-loop gains and limits; all zeros selects the
controller's built-in defaults.

damping.description:
Joint (`torque`) or Cartesian (`cartesian_impedance`) damping, seven
entries. Omitted requests the mode's own default.

eef_rotation.description:
`cartesian_impedance`: end-effector rotation parameters forwarded to
the controller.

force_direction.description:
`force_compliance`: which Cartesian directions (X, Y, Z, Rx, Ry, Rz)
the force loop acts on; `1` enables a direction, `0` disables it.

holder.description:
The arm lease holder issuing this command. Required only while somebody
holds the lease: with no lease held the field is ignored, and with one
held a request whose `holder` does not match is refused with 409.

mode.description: Which arm control mode to enter; selects which of the other fields apply.

stiffness.description:
Joint (`torque`) or Cartesian (`cartesian_impedance`) stiffness, seven
entries. Omitted requests the mode's own default.

target_force.description:
`force_compliance`: target contact force in newtons. Must not be
negative; any positive value is an active push, not a threshold.

vel_ratio.description:
Velocity ratio, as a backend-defined normalized ratio (`0.0..=1.0`).
Used by `position`, `torque`, `cartesian_impedance` and
`force_compliance`.

zero_wrist_roll.description:
`force_compliance`: command the wrist-roll joint (J7) to zero as part
of the entry anchor rather than freezing it in place.

ArmPreflightReport.description: Read-only assessment, not a reservation or authorization for future motion.

oneOf.description:
The INFO-level suggestion this state earns, when it earns one.

Additive and absent when it earns none. It is NOT a blocker and does
not affect `ready`: `blocking` lists what prevents an ordinary
position request, while this says what an operator would do next
about a machine that is working exactly as designed. The two never
overlap — an arm with a nonzero `error_code` is in `blocking` and
earns no advisory.

It is the same value as `state.advisory`, assigned from one
computation so the two cannot disagree.

blocking.description: Actionable reasons preventing a position-mode request.

commanded_gap_deg.description: Maximum absolute command/feedback difference, in degrees.

oneOf.description: Optional read-only board diagnostics; historical faults are not live errors.

feedback_advancing.description: Whether feedback advanced during the observation period.

initial_frame_serial.description: Frame serial before the 300 ms observation period.

max_velocity_deg_s.description: Maximum absolute feedback velocity, in degrees per second.

ready.description:
True only when no blocker to an ordinary position request was observed.
This does not determine whether recovery can be attempted.

warnings.description: Optional diagnostics unavailable or incomplete; not hidden as success.

ArmRecoverReport.description: Successful recovery to a measured-pose position hold.

recovered.description: True after the final clean-position confirmation and gap check.

state.description: State observed after confirming position mode.

ArmRecoverRequest.description: Explicit recovery command; ratios are normalized, not percentages.

ArmSide.description: Selects one of the two physical arms.

ArmSlot.description:
Either the device's own state or, when that device could not be
read, a [`SlotError`] naming the failure.

oneOf.description: The device answered; this is its state.
The device could not be read.

ArmSlots.description: The two arms' slots, keyed by side, and the operator lease over both.

a.description: Arm A, the robot's physical LEFT arm.

b.description: Arm B, the robot's physical RIGHT arm.

oneOf.description:
Who currently holds the arms, or `null` when they are free.

One lease covers both sides. Unlike the device slots this one never
degrades to an error: it is daemon-local state, not a device read. It
is also independent of the kill latch — a soft kill stops the arms but
does not take the lease away from whoever holds it.

An INFO-level suggestion about the state above, when it earns one.

Additive and absent when it does not, so a consumer that has never
heard of it reads exactly the state it always read.

This is the one field on this struct the arm BACKEND never fills: it
folds in the arm soft-kill latch, which is the daemon's own state and
not anything a controller reports, so it is attached where the daemon
hands an [`ArmState`] out ([`crate::D1::arm_state`],
[`crate::D1::arm_preflight`] and the `/v1/state` snapshot) and is
`None` on every read taken straight from the device. See
[`crate::arm_advisory`].

brakes_released.description:
Whether this daemon has forced this arm's holding brakes OPEN for hand
guiding (`POST /v1/arm/{side}/brake_release`) and not engaged them
since. While `true` nothing holds the arm but whoever is supporting
it; `GET /v1/arm/{side}/brake` has the window and who asked.

Like [`Self::advisory`], this is the daemon's own record and not
something the controller reports, so it is attached where the daemon
hands an [`ArmState`] out and is `false` on a read taken straight from
the device. It is NOT [`ArmMode::Release`], which is a controller mode.

command_joints.description: Last commanded joint positions in degrees.

controller_version.description:
The arm controller's firmware version, or `None` until it has been
read.

Reported identically on both sides because there is ONE controller
behind both arms. It is read once at startup from the vendor's
`VERSION` parameter — the same read the vendor's own SDK performs when
it connects — and it is what says which host-to-controller wire
generation the controller speaks.

error_code.description: Controller error code, zero when no error is reported.

feedback_temperature.description: Feedback joint temperatures in degrees Celsius.

feedback_velocity.description: Feedback joint velocities in degrees per second.

frame_miss_count.description:
`RT_IN.m_FrameMissCnt`: how many host command frames the controller
reckons it did not receive.

The controller's OWN measure of host-side delivery jitter, refreshed
every 200 control cycles, with the vendor's healthy band being below
20. It is the field that decides whether a stuttering arm is this
host's cadence or the controller's own scheduling — see
[`Self::sys_cycle_miss_count`] for the other half of that split.

max_frame_miss_count.description:
The high-water mark of [`Self::frame_miss_count`] since the controller
started. It never falls, so a zero here means an arm that has never
stuttered rather than one that is not stuttering right now.

protocol_mismatch.description:
Whether arm motion is currently REFUSED because the controller's
firmware generation and the daemon's configured `[arm] protocol`
disagree.

The two host-to-controller generations differ by a leading `[i32
serial]` in the joint-command record, and a controller on the other
generation does not reject the frame — it parses it shifted by one
element. Measured on d1-1 (controller `100343024`) on 2026-09-17: a
position-mode move under the older framing moved every joint toward
its NEIGHBOUR's target. So this is a refusal and not a warning, and it
is published here because an operator whose commands are being refused
needs to see why without reading the daemon's log.

`false` while the version has not been read, and `false` when
`[arm] allow_protocol_mismatch` is set for bench work.

stationary.description: Whether the arm reports low-speed/stationary motion.

sys_cycle_miss_count.description:
`RT_IN.m_SysCycMissCnt`: how many of the CONTROLLER's own realtime
cycles missed their deadline.

ArmToolSource.description: Where the tool registration one arm is holding came from.

ArmToolStatus.description:
What the daemon has registered on one arm, and where it came from.

The arm controller does not report its registered tool in feedback, so
this is the daemon's own record of what it last sent. It is the answer to
"is this arm compensating for the gripper it is actually wearing?", which
is otherwise only visible as a sagging wrist.

model.description:
The `"<maker>/<model>"` end-effector id, when the registration came
from the daemon's catalog. A client registration carries raw numbers
and no model name, so this is `null` for one.

source.description: Which of the two places the registration came from.

oneOf.description:
The values the controller was given, or `null` when nothing has been
registered on this side.

BatteryCell.description:
One battery pack of the mobile base, as the vendor's sensor push service
reports it.

Only the sensor-stream source produces these; the HTTP source has one
aggregate percentage and no per-pack detail, so a [`ChassisBattery`] from
it carries an empty `cells`.

age_ms.description:
How long ago this pack's reading was taken, in milliseconds.

`0` means the pack reported during the read that produced this state.
A larger value means it did not, and the daemon is still reporting the
last value that pack sent.

The base pushes one pack per frame, so a read of the push service can
legitimately come back with only one of the two packs in it -- the
service serves one client at a time and evicts the previous one, and a
read that is cut short that way is not evidence that a pack is gone.
Dropping the missing pack from the reading made the published charge
oscillate: on the D1 mobile base measured on 2026-09-19, `cells`
alternated between two packs and one every few seconds and the pack
aggregate followed it. So the last reading of each pack is retained
for a bounded time and published with its age, which is the fact a
consumer needs in order to decide whether to trust it.

charge_status.description:
The pack's raw `charge_status` field exactly as the vendor's sensor
push service sent it. `0` discharging and `1` charging are the only two
the vendor documents.

charging.description:
Whether this pack reports current flowing in: `true` for the vendor's
documented `charge_status` 1, `false` for the documented 0, and `null`
for any other value the pack reports.

Never `false` for an undocumented code. The D1 mobile base measured on
2026-09-09 reports `charge_status = 2`, which the vendor documents
nowhere; answering `false` there would tell an operator the pack is not
charging when nothing measured says so.

current.description: Pack current, in the vendor's own raw unit.

max_temperature.description:
This pack's highest cell temperature, in the vendor's own raw unit
(degrees Celsius in every reading measured so far).

remaining_capacity.description: Remaining capacity, in the vendor's own raw unit.

serial.description: The vendor's `serial_number`: 0 is pack 1, 1 is pack 2.

soc_percent.description: This pack's state of charge, as a percentage.

a.description: Arm A target joint angles in degrees, seven joints.

b.description: Arm B target joint angles in degrees, seven joints.

wait.description: Block until both arms report arrival (up to 30 s).

ChargeBasis.description:
Where the daemon's `charging` answer came from, or that it has no source.

The two mobile-base firmware generations report charge over different
transports and only one of them is right for a given base, so the evidence
travels with the answer rather than being left for a consumer to guess.

ChargeDock.description:
The charging-dock scene and waypoint written through the map resource's
`charging_dock` sub-resource, later used by `charge` (vendor
`sendChargeCmd`).

ChargeDockReadStatus.description: Outcome of the latest vendor charging-dock read, independent of fallback provenance.

ChargingDockPut.description:
`PUT /v1/chassis/maps/{scene}/charging_dock`.

The scene is the path segment, so only the waypoint is in the body: it
names which of that map's waypoints the mobile base treats as its
charging dock.

point_id.description: Vendor point identifier of the dock within that scene.

ChassisApplicationState.description: What can be proven about application to the running controller.

ChassisBattery.description:
`GET /v1/chassis/battery`.

The single number this route has always returned, plus the reading it was
taken from: which transport supplied it, and the per-pack detail when that
transport reports any.  The two mobile-base firmware generations read the
battery over different transports, so a consumer that must tell "no
reading" from "a reading of zero" reads `source` and `percent` rather than
`battery_percent` alone.

battery_percent.description: Battery percentage, or `-1` when the chassis did not report one.

cells.description: The per-pack readings, empty on a source that has none.

charging.description:
Whether the base is charging: `true` and `false` only on positive
evidence, `null` when the only evidence is a code the vendor
documents nowhere or when there is none at all.

Never `false` for an undocumented pack code. Read `basis` to see why
a `null` is null.

charging_status_raw.description:
The vendor HTTP API's `chargingStatus` string exactly as it arrived,
or `null` on a mobile-base firmware generation whose `chargingStatus`
is a dead constant and is therefore not read at all.

percent.description: The charge from that source, or `null` when it could not be read.

source.description: `http` or `sensor-stream`: where the charge is supposed to come from.

ChassisBatteryReading.description:
The mobile base's battery reading, and which source it came from.

The two mobile-base firmware generations report the battery over different
transports, and only one of them is right for a given base: the older
generation's HTTP `powerPercentage` field, or the newer generation's TCP
sensor push service. This value says which source was used, so a consumer
can tell "no reading" from "a reading of zero" and can see when a base's
charge is coming from somewhere other than where it expects.

[`ChassisState::battery_percent`] is filled from the SELECTED source and
stays the single number a consumer that wants only a number reads.

basis.description:
Which reading `charging` came from; [`ChargeBasis::None`] whenever
`charging` is `null`.

cells.description: The per-pack readings, when the source provides them.

charging.description:
Whether the pack reports charging, or `None` when the selected source
does not say (the older generation's `chargingStatus` field, which
stopped tracking charge after the vendor's battery swap, is not read).

charging_status_raw.description:
The vendor HTTP API's `chargingStatus` string exactly as it arrived,
when this base's generation still serves a live one and it was read.
`null` on a generation whose `chargingStatus` is known dead, which is
not consulted at all.

percent.description:
The charge as a percentage, or `None` when the selected source could
not be read. It is never filled from the other source: a generation
whose HTTP gauge reads a constant 0 would otherwise publish 0 % as a
real charge.

ChassisCatalogRequest.description:
Exactly seven supported reads. No caller-selected endpoint is accepted.

This is where a fixed, parameterless or identifier-selected vendor
DOCUMENT read belongs, rather than a route of its own: the daemon's own
chassis routes publish the daemon's model of the base (its state, its
navigation, its settings), while these publish a vendor document verbatim,
with its provenance, for a consumer that needs the vendor's own wording.
`RosStatus` and `ChargingStatToday` are read-only reads of exactly that
shape, which is why they are variants here.

oneOf.description: Saved tasks for an explicitly named scene.
Timed tasks for an explicitly named scene.
A saved plan within an explicitly named scene.
Vendor cyclic-task monitor settings, not host CPU telemetry.
Vendor USB inventory. Does not mount or write devices.

Whether the vendor web application currently holds its own connection
to the base's ROS side: `{"connected": <bool>}`.

Computed inside the web application from three in-process checks, so
it touches neither the chassis nor the robot. It is the cheapest
statement the web application can make about its link to the base, and
it is a DIFFERENT fact from the daemon's own reachability: a web
application that answers this read with `false` is up while its ROS
side is not.

Served only by the `corona-2026` mobile-base firmware generation's web
application; a `gs-2026` base refuses this read.

The chassis PC's charging tally for its own current date:
`{"date", "chargeCount", "totalDuration", "totalDurationFormatted"}`.

`date` is the chassis PC's date as `yyyy-MM-dd`, `chargeCount` a
count of charging sessions, `totalDuration` a number of MILLISECONDS,
and `totalDurationFormatted` that duration as the vendor's own Chinese
string. A day with no record reads as zeros and the literal `0分钟`
rather than as an error.

Served only by the `corona-2026` mobile-base firmware generation's web
application; a `gs-2026` base refuses this read.

ChassisCatalogSnapshot.description: A received vendor document. Its schema may differ by firmware generation.

received_at_unix_ms.description: Unix milliseconds when the daemon received the document.

request.description: Exact selector used for this reading; never infer a current scene.

source.description: Fixed vendor HTTP endpoint that supplied the value.

value.description: Complete decoded result, including unknown fields and explicit null.

ChassisChargeState.description:
Everything the daemon knows about the mobile base's charging, in one
object: where the base is in its docking routine, whether automatic
charging is the mode it is in, what its battery packs say about current
flow, and which waypoint pressing "charge" would send it to.

The four are separate fields because they are four different measurements
that routinely disagree, and folding them into one flag is what makes an
operator guess. The vendor's own sequence, from its example program
`7.add_charge.py`, is: start automatic charging, and `workMode` goes 1 to 2
while `dockStatus` goes 0 to 1; docking completes and `dockStatus` becomes
2; the base leaves and `dockStatus` goes 3 then 0 while `workMode` returns
to 1. Through all of that, whether current is actually flowing is reported
only by the battery pack.

auto_charging.description:
Whether the base's work mode is the vendor's automatic-charging mode
(`workMode == 2`).

This is the base's MODE, not a measurement of current: a base can sit
in `workMode` 2 having failed to reach its dock.

charging.description:
Whether the base is charging: `true` only on positive evidence,
`false` only on positive evidence, and `null` when the only evidence
is a code nothing documents or when there is no evidence at all.

An undocumented pack code is NEVER folded into `false`. A consumer
that must show something for `null` should show "unknown", not "not
charging"; [`Self::basis`] says why it is `null`.

dock.description: The docking phase, decoded from the vendor's `dockStatus`.

oneOf.description:
The scene and waypoint the base charges at, when it can be determined.

Read back from the mobile base itself where the base answers the
vendor's `getChargeInfo` endpoint, and otherwise from the value this
daemon process last wrote successfully through the map resource's
`charging_dock` sub-resource. [`Self::dock_point_source`] says which of
the two this is. `null` means neither was available — which is not the
same as "no dock is configured", and a `charge` command may still be
refused with the `dock_unconfigured` refusal kind.

dock_raw.description:
The vendor's `dockStatus` string exactly as it arrived, or `null` when
the base reported no such field.

dock_read_status.description: Latest read outcome; empty or malformed data never proves unconfigured.

pack_raw.description:
The raw `charge_status` integer that decided [`Self::pack`], or `null`
when no pack reported.

ChassisCommonFileDelete.description: Delete one exact listed file after fresh current-content comparison.

expected_revision.description: Opaque selector+content revision from a present reading.

ChassisCommonFileDownloadEvidence.description: Header and byte-count evidence from the exact download request.

ChassisControlReport.description:
What one control verb did, and the state the base was in afterwards.

The steps are here because a control verb is not always one vendor call:
entering remote control from navigation mode closes navigation, waits for
the base to actually leave that mode, and only then enters remote control.
An operator interface that shows only the end state cannot tell that apart
from a single call, and an operator who has just lost a navigation goal
deserves to be told that this is what took it.

control.description:
The control state after the last step: vendor readings plus this
daemon's motor command memory. Motors have no physical readback,
and this report does not verify physical movement.

steps.description: What the daemon sent to the base, in the order it sent it.

ChassisControlState.description:
Everything the daemon knows about WHICH CONTROLLER may drive the mobile
base: the mode it is in, what that mode permits, and which control verbs
are legal from it.

The mobile base has exactly one control mode at a time and every motion
path is gated on it, but the vendor publishes that only as a bare
`workMode` digit and enforces it by IGNORING commands: outside its
remote-control mode the base answers a jog with HTTP 200 and does not
move. This object is the daemon's answer to "what state is the base in,
what can I do from here, and why not" in one read, so that an operator
interface never has to infer it from a digit or from a command that
silently did nothing.

The five vendor modes are the vendor's own, taken from its web
application's own translation table: `0` navigation closed, `1`
navigation, `2` automatic charging, `3` mapping, `4` remote control.

auto_status_raw.description:
The vendor's `autoStatus` string exactly as it arrived, whatever mode
the base is in, or `null` when the base reported no such field.

bumper.description:
Whether a bumper input is latched: the same fact as
[`ChassisState::bumper_pressed`], which is the OR of the vendor's
`stripStatus` and `stopStatus` fields.

can_hand_drive.description:
Whether the reported control preconditions permit sending a jog or
nonzero velocity command, before the separate software stop gate.

True only when the base is in remote-control mode, is not reported in standby,
has its emergency switch released, and has not had its motors released
by this daemon. [`MotorState::Unknown`] does not block: nothing on the
base reports the motor state, so refusing on it would make hand-drive
permanently unavailable on a daemon that has just started. Unknown
standby also does not block. A true value is not proof of physical
movement: motor command memory can be stale, and the base's bumper
interlock can stop motion without blocking command transmission.
The daemon's software stop latch can still refuse the request.

emergency_switch.description:
Whether the base's physical emergency-stop input reads as pressed.

The same fact as [`ChassisState::emergency_stop`], repeated here so
that `GET /v1/chassis/control` answers every precondition of driving
the base without a second read.

hand_drive_blockers.description:
Every precondition of [`Self::can_hand_drive`] that is not met, each
with the sentence that says what clears it. Empty when
`can_hand_drive` is true.

local_goal_id.description:
Which route-network point the base is currently driving to, as the
vendor's `localGoalId` names it, or `null` when it is driving to none.

This is the base's OWN answer about its own trip, and it is the only
one that survives this daemon restarting: the daemon's `navigate`
handles (`NavId`) are process-local, so after a restart -- or for a
trip somebody started from the base's own web interface -- this is the
only identification of what is running.

`"0"` is normalised to `null` here. It is the vendor's idle sentinel,
measured on D1 #1 while the base was doing nothing, and it cannot
collide with a real point: route-network point identifiers are
zero-padded to four digits (`"0001"`, `"0007"`), so a bare `"0"` is
never one of them. An empty string is normalised the same way. The
unnormalised value is in [`Self::local_goal_id_raw`], so the
normalisation destroys nothing.

local_goal_id_raw.description:
The vendor's `localGoalId` exactly as it arrived, or `null` when the
base sent the field empty or did not send it at all.

mode.description: The vendor work mode the base is in.

motors.description:
This daemon's last successful motor-engagement write, or unknown.
This is command memory, not a reading of the motors' physical state.

motors_source.description:
Where [`Self::motors`] came from. It is never a reading FROM the base:
the base publishes no motor-lock field at all.

navigation.description:
The navigation state, decoded from `autoStatus` while the base is in
navigation mode and [`NavigationState::Off`] otherwise.

remote_control.description:
Whether that mode is the vendor's remote-control mode (`workMode`
`4`), which is the only mode in which the base acts on a jog or a
velocity command.

standby.description:
Whether the base is in its standby (sleep) state: `true` for the
vendor's documented `standbyStatus` 1, `false` for the documented 0,
and `null` when the base reported no such field or a value the vendor
documents nowhere.

A standby base stops acting on remote-control commands. It is woken
over the base's own ROS layer (`SleepCtrl`), which has no HTTP verb,
so this daemon reports the state and cannot change it.

standby_raw.description:
The vendor's `standbyStatus` string exactly as it arrived, or `null`
when the base reported no such field.

stop_status_raw.description:
The vendor's `stopStatus` string exactly as it arrived, or `null`.

The vendor publishes NO dictionary for this field and its own programs
read it three incompatible ways, so the daemon folds any non-zero
value into [`Self::bumper`] and publishes the raw value here rather
than inventing a meaning for it.

strip_status_raw.description:
The vendor's `stripStatus` string exactly as it arrived, or `null`.
This is the anti-collision bumper strip, `0` not triggered and `1`
triggered, cleared by `POST /v1/chassis/remove_strip`.

transitions.description:
Which control verbs are legal from this state, and why the others are
not.

This describes the MOBILE BASE's own mode machine and nothing else.
The daemon's soft-kill latch is a separate gate that can still refuse
an `allowed: true` verb with the `kill_latched` failure kind; read
`/v1/state`'s `soft_killed` for that.

ChassisParam.description:
One chassis parameter write, as `POST /v1/chassis/set_params` and the
WebSocket `chassis.set_params` method take it.

The vendor's `setParams` endpoint writes one of SIX settings on the mobile
base, each into its own YAML file on the chassis PC. This is the typed
form of that request: `{"kind": "max", "value": 0.3}`,
`{"kind": "low_or_strong", "value": 0.4}`, `{"kind": "slope", "value":
0.5}`, `{"kind": "narrow", "value": 0.4}`, `{"kind": "dist_stop",
"value": 0.3}`, or `{"kind": "footprint", "value": [[x, y], [x, y],
[x, y], [x, y]]}`.

[`ChassisParam::Narrow`] is accepted by this type and REFUSED by the
daemon; see its own documentation for why.

oneOf.description:
The base's maximum driving speed, in metres per second, written as
`max_linear_vel` into both of the chassis driver's parameter files.
The vendor accepts up to and including 1.2.

value.description:
The base's maximum driving speed, in metres per second, written as
`max_linear_vel` into both of the chassis driver's parameter files.
The vendor accepts up to and including 1.2.

oneOf.description:
The local planner's speed limit inside the slow-down / strong-light
zone, in metres per second, written as `max_vel_x` into
`navigator/teb_path_low_or_strong.yaml`. The vendor range-checks
nothing; the daemon requires a finite positive number.

value.description:
The local planner's speed limit inside the slow-down / strong-light
zone, in metres per second, written as `max_vel_x` into
`navigator/teb_path_low_or_strong.yaml`. The vendor range-checks
nothing; the daemon requires a finite positive number.

oneOf.description:
The local planner's speed limit inside a slope zone, in metres per
second, written as `max_vel_x` into `navigator/teb_path_slope.yaml`.
The vendor range-checks nothing; the daemon requires a finite
positive number.

value.description:
The local planner's speed limit inside a slope zone, in metres per
second, written as `max_vel_x` into `navigator/teb_path_slope.yaml`.
The vendor range-checks nothing; the daemon requires a finite
positive number.

oneOf.description:
Nominally the local planner's speed limit inside a narrow passage —
**refused by the daemon, and not sent**.

The vendor's writer for this type targets
`navigator/teb_path_stop.yaml` while its own reader reports the
`narrow` value out of `navigator/teb_path_narrow.yaml`, so the write
can never be read back. The variant exists so that asking for it is
answered with that reason rather than with "unknown kind".

Nominally the local planner's speed limit inside a narrow passage —
**refused by the daemon, and not sent**.

The vendor's writer for this type targets
`navigator/teb_path_stop.yaml` while its own reader reports the
`narrow` value out of `navigator/teb_path_narrow.yaml`, so the write
can never be read back. The variant exists so that asking for it is
answered with that reason rather than with "unknown kind".

oneOf.description:
The charging-dock stop distance, in metres, written as
`lidar_docking.dist_stop` into `docking/lidar_dock.yaml`. The vendor
accepts the inclusive range 0.225 to 0.425.

value.description:
The charging-dock stop distance, in metres, written as
`lidar_docking.dist_stop` into `docking/lidar_dock.yaml`. The vendor

The base's footprint polygon: four `[x, y]` corners, in metres,
written as `footprint` into `navigator/costmap_params.yaml` and as

ChassisParamApplies.description:
When a written [`ChassisParam`] starts being used by the mobile base.

Every `setParams` type writes a YAML file under the vendor's
`<workspace>/install/share/robot_bringup/param/` and nothing more: no
binary in the vendor's installed autonomy tree contains any of those file
names, so no running node re-reads one. The written value therefore
reaches the base only when the node whose launch file loads that YAML with
`<rosparam command="load">` is started again — and WHICH node that is
differs per type, which is why this is an enumeration and not a flag.

[`ChassisParamApplies::NoKnownReader`] is not a restart at all: the write
lands in a file that no launch file in the installed tree loads, so no
restart makes it take effect.

ChassisSetParamsReport.description:
What one [`ChassisParam`] write did.

Three fields exist because a write can be accepted and still change
nothing, in three independent ways: the older mobile-base firmware
generation serves `setParams` and ignores what it is told
([`ChassisSetParamsReport::effective`]); the vendor writes a YAML file and
no running node re-reads it, so the value waits for a restart, and for
WHICH restart depends on the parameter
([`ChassisSetParamsReport::applies_when`]); and for one parameter no node
reads the written file at all. All of it travels with the response rather
than being left for the caller to know.

Whether this generation's firmware acts on this endpoint at all.
`false` means the request was accepted and will do nothing.

The mobile-base firmware generation the write was sent to, as
[`ChassisVendorInfo::generation`] spells it.

kind.description: The parameter that was written, as [`ChassisParam::kind`] spells it.

A one-line statement of the conditions above, for an operator reading
the response by hand.

value.description: The exact string sent as the vendor's `value`.

vendor_file.description:
The vendor YAML file the write lands in, relative to the chassis PC's
`<workspace>/install/share/robot_bringup/param/`, or an empty string
when it is not established. A parameter written into two files names
both, separated by `", "`.

ChassisSpeedCap.description:
The effective linear speed cap, and the two caps it was chosen between.

The mobile base saturates a velocity command silently: its navigation
stack carries its own `max_linear_vel`, and a `sendToMove` above that
value is accepted, answered with success, and then driven at the base's
own cap instead. A single number in an operator interface is therefore not
enough -- "I asked for 0.5 m/s and the base said yes" is true and useless.
This structure reports the number a command is actually clamped to, both
inputs to that choice, and which one bound.

daemon_linear_m_s.description: This daemon's pinned safety limit, independent of any base.

effective_linear_m_s.description:
The cap velocity commands are clamped to: the lower of the two below,
or the daemon's own when the base's could not be read.

vendor_linear_m_s.description:
The base's own declared maximum, or null when it could not be read.

Read from the `max` field of the vendor's saved speed settings. It is
a per-generation and per-unit value -- the deployed navigation stack of
one base declares 0.3 where another declares 1.0 -- so it is read from
the base rather than pinned here.

vendor_read_error.description: Why the base's declared maximum is absent, or null when it was read.

ChassisSpeedCapSource.description: Which of the two linear speed caps turned out to be the binding one.

ChassisSpeedReadbackScope.description: The limited source observed after an accepted profile save.

ChassisSpeedSave.description: Conditional save of one profile through setSpeedSetting, not setParams.

expected.description: Complete original getSpeedSetting object, including unknown fields.

profile.description: Exact profile; narrow is rejected before any manufacturer write.

value.description: Finite positive saved proposal. No verified vendor upper bound is claimed.
