ChassisState.description:
Chassis feedback, including whether the mobile base is there at all.

A D1 is regularly run with its vendor chassis powered off — on external
power, using only the lift, arms, torso and head. The chassis controller is
then a dead HTTP origin, and every request to it costs a full connect
timeout. [`ChassisState::available`] is the daemon's standing answer to
"is the base there", decided by a bounded startup probe and re-checked on a
timer, so a caller can skip its chassis steps outright rather than
discovering the absence one timeout at a time.

availability_reason.description:
Why [`ChassisState::available`] holds its current value: the transport
error for an absent base, the configuration for one declared absent,
and a short confirmation for a reachable one.

available.description:
Whether the chassis controller answered the last availability check.

`false` means every chassis command and query is refused immediately
with `unavailable` and NOTHING is sent to the network; the rest of this
structure is then the default reading, not a measurement. Consumers
that orchestrate the robot should read this field and skip their
chassis steps rather than issuing commands that cannot succeed.

battery.description:
The battery reading and which source it came from. `battery_percent`
above is this reading's percentage, or `-1.0` when it has none.

charge.description:
The base's charging state: docking phase, automatic-charging mode,
what the packs report, and which waypoint it charges at.

This is the field an operator interface reads to answer "what state is
the base in, and what would pressing charge do"; `work_mode` above
carries only the first half of that.

control.description:
Which controller may drive the base: the vendor work mode it is in,
whether control preconditions permit sending a jog, and which control verbs are
legal from here.

`work_mode` above is the bare digit this object decodes; everything
used by the control precondition checks -- the mode, standby state,
emergency switch and motor command memory -- travels here together.
Permission to send is not evidence that the base physically moved.

emergency_stop.description: Whether the chassis emergency stop is active.

last_probe_unix_ms.description:
Milliseconds since the UNIX epoch at which the last availability check
settled, or `0` when none has run (a backend that does not probe).

oneOf.description:
Latest finite measured map coordinates; absent when no complete pose
was reported. Heading is not inferred from motion or a command.

speed_cap.description:
The linear speed cap velocity commands are actually clamped to, and
which of the two caps it came from.

status_json.description: Full vendor status JSON, preserved for frontend consumers.

vendor.description: The vendor's identity and firmware/software build strings.

ChassisTransition.description:
Whether one [`ControlVerb`] is legal from the state the base is in, and
why.

`reason` is filled in BOTH cases, because both are things a consumer has
to show: for a refused verb it says which state refused it, and for an
allowed verb that does more than one thing it says what the daemon will
actually do.

allowed.description: Whether the daemon will attempt it from the current state.

reason.description: Why it is refused, or what an allowed verb will do.

verb.description: The verb this row is about.

ChassisUltrasonic.description:
The mobile base's ultrasonic proximity ring, as the daemon last read it.

This is a HARDWARE-CHECK reading. The daemon does not brake, stop or
re-route the base on it and nothing here is a safety interlock; it exists
so an operator can see whether the ring is working and what it sees.

The ring is published only by the vendor's TCP sensor push service, which
one mobile-base firmware generation serves and the other does not, so
"this base cannot report sonar" is a normal answer and is reported as
[`ChassisUltrasonic::supported`] `false` with a stated
[`ChassisUltrasonic::reason`] rather than as an error or as an empty
reading that looks like a silent ring.

age_ms.description:
How long ago the newest frame behind this reading was read, in
milliseconds, or `null` when there is no reading.

channels.description:
One entry per channel the daemon has a reading for, ordered by index.
Empty whenever there is no reading.

frame_id.description:
The vendor frame's source identifier; the D1 mobile base sends
`sonar_array`. `null` when there is no reading.

link.description:
How the daemon is reading the base's sensor push service right now,
and therefore how live the rest of this reading is.

reason.description:
Empty when a reading was obtained. Otherwise one sentence saying why
there is none — an unsupported generation, an unplaceable one, or the
transport failure from the attempted read.

seq.description:
The vendor frame's global sequence number, or `null` when there is no
reading.

source.description:
Where the reading came from: `sensor-stream`, or `none` when there is
no reading.

stamp_s.description:
The vendor frame's timestamp in seconds, or `null` when there is no
reading.

supported.description:
Whether this base can report an ultrasonic ring at all: whether its
mobile-base firmware generation serves the sensor push service.

`false` is a statement about the base, not about this read. A base
that is supported but whose service could not be reached has
`supported` `true`, a `source` of `none`, and the transport failure in
`reason`.

omega.description: Angular velocity in radians per second; positive is counter-clockwise.

vx.description: Forward velocity in metres per second; negative is reverse.

ChassisVendorInfo.description:
The mobile base's vendor-reported identity and firmware/software build
strings, as returned by the chassis controller's `getRobotInfo` endpoint.

These fields are informational only (nothing in this core acts on them);
they exist so that a vendor identity or firmware change on the chassis PC
— otherwise silent, since the daemon only ever polls state — is observable
through the same state and telemetry surfaces as any other chassis
reading.

generation.description:
Which generation of the vendor's mobile-base firmware the identity and
version strings below were decided to belong to: `gs-2026`,
`corona-2026`, or `unknown` for an identity this firmware version
cannot place (including a base that has not answered yet).

Unlike the five raw strings, this one the daemon DOES act on: it
decides which source the battery reading comes from, and whether a
speed command or a parameter write can be expected to have any effect.

master_version.description: Vendor `masterVersion`, the chassis controller's firmware build.

robot_no.description: Vendor `robotNo`, the chassis PC's own identity string.

web_version.description: Vendor `webVersion`, the chassis PC's web-application build.

CheckReport.description: Wire-level result of checking one or both arm poses.

valid.description: Whether the supplied pose is accepted by the guard.

ClampReport.description: Wire-level result of clamping one arm pose to its URDF limits.

changed.description: Whether any joint differs exactly from its supplied value.

clamped_deg.description: The seven clamped joint angles in degrees, or an empty vector for an invalid request.

ControlStep.description: One thing the daemon did while carrying out a control verb.

action.description:
What was done, as a stable word: `close_navigation`, `settle`,
`enter_remote_control`, `leave_remote_control`, `start_navigation`,
`engage_motors`, `release_motors`, `read_back`.

detail.description:
The detail of that step: the vendor call that was sent, how long a
settle waited, or what the read-back saw.

ControlVerb.description:
One control verb of the mobile base's mode machine.

These are the verbs that change WHICH controller may drive the base, as
opposed to the verbs that drive it. They are named here rather than only
as routes so that [`ChassisControlState::transitions`] can say which of
them are legal from the state the base is in right now.

ControllerFault.description:
One controller fault scanned from the vendor `LOG.txt` tail.

The originating log line is kept verbatim in `raw` because a fault log is
inherently free-form; the other fields are the structured extraction.

arm.description: The arm the fault names, if any (e.g. `arm0`).

codes.description: Servo error codes carried by the line (e.g. `0xff51`), in order.

timestamp.description: The log line's own timestamp token (e.g. `00:15:38`).

ControllerHealth.description:
Derived health of the arm controller.

Health is DERIVED from the structured anatomy (process/module presence,
slave AL states, recent fault severity) — never from mere output stability.

state.description: The conversation state the eye indicator should show.

ConversationState.description: Conversation phase shown by the eye LEDs.

Device.description: A D1 device for kill-latch and error reporting purposes.

DockPhase.description:
The automatic-charging (docking) phase the mobile base reports.

This is the daemon's typed reading of the vendor's `dockStatus` field. It
says where the base is in its docking routine and says NOTHING about
whether current is flowing — only the battery pack reports that, which is
why [`ChassisChargeState`] carries the two side by side.

note.description: An operator's note to store with the dump.

pinned.description:
Whether to pin it against retention immediately. Omitted means not
pinned.

post_trigger_s.description:
Seconds to wait after the trigger before copying the ring. Omitted
means `0`: an operator asking for a dump is asking about what has
ALREADY happened, and a request that blocked for five seconds would
look like a hung daemon.

name.description:
The file's name inside the dump directory, e.g.
`statelog.arm.a.jsonl`. A dump directory is flat, so this is one path
segment and never carries a `/`. It is also the only name
[`Recorder::read_file`] accepts for this dump.

records.description: Lines in the file for a JSON Lines file, `null` for anything else.

sha256.description:
Lowercase hex SHA-256 of the file's bytes, so a dump copied off the
robot can be checked without trusting the copy.

DumpManifest.description:
A dump's `manifest.json`, which is also what the API answers with.

One type for the file and the wire on purpose: the file IS the record, and
a second shape for the API would be a second thing to keep true.

bytes.description: The sum of `files[].bytes`; what this dump costs the retention budget.

complete.description:
Whether the second phase finished. `false` means the daemon was
stopped between the trigger and the copy: `snapshot.json` is there and
the ring is not.

created_ts.description: When the dump was created, UTC RFC 3339 with millisecond precision.

daemon_version.description: The daemon version that wrote it.

files.description: Every file in the dump, `manifest.json` itself excluded.

id.description:
The dump's identifier and its directory name: a sortable UTC timestamp
and a short suffix, e.g. `20260920T060312Z-a1b2`.

pinned.description: Whether retention may evict this dump. A pinned dump never is.

post_trigger_s.description: Seconds waited after the trigger before the ring was copied.

pre_trigger.description: The history the ring gave it.

session.description:
The daemon run that wrote it — the same token the state log's `meta`
records carry, so a dump and a ring can be tied to one run.

v.description: Manifest version; [`MANIFEST_VERSION`] for anything this daemon wrote.

DumpNamespace.description: How far back one namespace's copied ring reaches.

newest_ts.description: The `ts` of the last record, or `null` when the file holds none.

oldest_ts.description: The `ts` of the first record, or `null` when the file holds none.

records.description: Records in it, the `meta` segment headers included.

segments.description: Segments concatenated into this namespace's file.

DumpPreTrigger.description:
What the ring gave this dump: the history that existed BEFORE the trigger.

This is the part of a dump that cannot be reconstructed afterwards, so the
manifest states its extent rather than leaving a reader to measure it.

namespaces.description:
One entry per namespace that had anything recorded, in the state log's
own stable namespace order.

statelog_dir.description:
The state-log root the ring was copied from, or `null` when no
recorder was running and the dump carries no ring at all.

DumpTrigger.description: One trigger: what raised it, when, and what it saw.

detail.description:
What the detector saw, in one sentence, or `null` when the kind says
everything there is to say. Prose for a human; branch on `kind`.

ts.description: When it was observed, UTC RFC 3339 with millisecond precision.

DumpUpdate.description:
`PATCH /v1/recorder/dumps/{id}`: the fields of one dump an operator may
change.

Which dump is not in the body: it is the `{id}` of the path, because a
dump is a resource this daemon owns and a PATCH addresses the resource it
is sent to. A body that could name a second dump would be a body that can
disagree with the path.

pinned.description: Whether retention may evict this dump. Omitted leaves it alone.

ErrorEnvelope.description: The failure envelope. `data` is always null; `message` always carries the daemon's own or the mobile base's error text; `kind` is always present and is the stable machine word to branch on; `code` is the mobile base's own numeric response code and is present only when the failure came from the base. Branch on `kind`, never on `message`. `advisory` is present only when the refusal knows the next step, and is absent otherwise.

code.description: The mobile base's numeric response code, or null when the failure did not come from the base.

ErrorEnvelope.title: ErrorEnvelope

ErrorKind.description:
A stable machine word for one failure, independent of its wording.

Every error this daemon returns carries one of these, and a consumer
branches on it rather than on the prose in `message`, which is the vendor's
or the daemon's own sentence and is free to change. The values fall into
two groups: the daemon's own conditions, and the mobile base's, which are
the vendor response codes classified into what an operator can do about
them.

EtherCatMaster.description:
One EtherCAT master and its ring (from `ethercat master` + `ethercat
slaves`).

link_up.description: Whether the main Ethernet link is up.

slave_count.description: Number of slaves the master reports on its ring.

slaves.description: The slaves attached to this master, in ring order.

EtherCatSlave.description: One EtherCAT slave on a master's ring (from `ethercat slaves`).

alias.description: Alias/address token as printed by the tool (e.g. `0:3`).

ExpressionList.description: The expression names and raw catalog types in index order.

ExpressionResult.description: Result shape used by the expression service facade.

success.description: Whether the request played through to its resolved loop count.

EyeCmdRequest.description:
The advertised request body of `POST /v1/eyes/cmd`.

This is a *flattened, advertise-only* view of [`d1fw_core::EyeCommand`],
whose `#[serde(flatten)]` of the tagged [`d1fw_core::EyeEffect`] enum
emitted an `allOf` over a `oneOf` — the shape `openapi-python-client`
silently drops (it removed the `EyeCommand` model and skipped the
endpoint). The daemon still deserializes the wire body into `EyeCommand`;
nothing deserializes into this struct. `target` and `effect` are required,
every colour/timing field is optional and applies only to the effects that
name it.

delay_ms.description: Delay between steps in milliseconds. Used by `breathing` and `running`.

effect.description: Which eye LED effect to run; selects which of the other fields apply.

step.description:
Breathing step size or running-light window length. Used by
`breathing` and `running`.

target.description: Which eye strips the effect addresses.

EyeTarget.description: Selects which eye LED strip receives an effect.

percent.description:
Battery percentage `0..=100`, clamped into that range.  `null` clears
the gauge.  Non-finite values may also be sent as the strings `nan`,
`inf` or `-inf`, which JSON itself cannot represent.

loops.description:
Loop count; omitted means `0`, which defers to the document's own
loop policy.  The service ceiling is 20 loops.

name.description: Catalog expression name, as listed by `GET /v1/eyes/list_expressions`.

EyesPixelRequest.description:
One frozen-window single-pixel placement request.

`index` is the LED index as the eye controller counts the strip
(`0..=17`), `target` names one eye (`left` or `right`; `both` is refused
because the two strips do not run a `BOTH`-addressed window in phase), and
`delay_ms` is the window speed in milliseconds per index, defaulting to
the measured 100 ms.

delay_ms.description:
Window speed in milliseconds per index; omitted selects the measured
100 ms default.

target.description: Which eye strip to place the pixel on; `both` is refused.

EyesPlaybackState.description: Live state for a named eye-expression playback.

elapsed_ms.description: Wall-clock milliseconds elapsed since playback started.

name.description: Catalog entry name resolved for the playback.

total_ms.description: Total wall-clock playback duration in milliseconds.

EyesSlot.description:
Either the device's own state or, when that device could not be
read, a [`SlotError`] naming the failure.

oneOf.description: The device answered; this is its state.
The device could not be read.

initialized.description: Whether the controller has completed its initialization sequence.

last_effect.description: Last effect name reported by the controller, if any.

mode.description: Current controller mode, such as `manual` or `off`.

oneOf.description: The named expression currently being played, if any.

GripPreset.description:
Named grip presets for a gripper stroke.

A preset is two numbers the backend configures per robot (see
[`GripPresets`]): the torque at which the closing stroke stops squeezing
what it has met, and the standing preload it then holds with. `firm` is
the default of a stroke that names nothing.

GripRequest.description:
How hard a closing stroke squeezes and holds what it meets.

At most one of the two fields is given: a named [`GripPreset`], or an
explicit standing preload in motor radians (which keeps the `firm`
preset's stop torque). Neither means the backend's configured default,
`firm`. Carried by [`GripperTarget`] and by a bare `close`.

oneOf.description: A named preset.

grip_preload_rad.description: An explicit standing preload, in motor radians.

GripperFaultReport.description:
What one gripper motor reports after a clear-fault attempt.

A DM motor that has latched a fault swallows position commands until it is
cleared, and until 2026-09-22 nothing in this daemon could ask it to let
go: every stroke after the fault was accepted, ended immediately as
`fault`, and the only recovery was a power cycle of the gripper. This is
what `POST /v1/gripper/{side}/clear_fault` answers with.

cleared.description:
Whether the motor is STILL reporting a fault.

`false` is the success case. `true` means the clear did not take:
`coil_over_temperature` cannot be cleared in software until the coil
has cooled, and a motor that re-faults instantly has something else
wrong with it.

fault_code.description: The fault still standing, when `cleared` is `false`.

status.description:
The motor's decoded status AFTER the clear: `disabled`, `enabled`, one
of the fault names, or `unknown`.

status_nibble.description: The raw status nibble the name was decoded from, `0x0..=0xf`.

coil_c.description: Coil temperature in °C from a live reading, when one was taken.

fault_code.description:
Which fault the motor is reporting, when `kind` is `fault`: one of
`over_voltage`, `under_voltage`, `over_current`,
`mos_over_temperature`, `coil_over_temperature`,
`communication_lost`, `overload` or `unknown`.

`null` when the gripper is not faulted, and also when the backend has
no reading to decode one from. A bare `kind: fault` told an operator
only that something was wrong; the cause is the difference between
"let the coil cool" (`coil_over_temperature` does not clear in
software at all) and "clear it and carry on".

grip_preload_rad.description:
Standing preload the hold keeps, in motor radians; zero when nothing
is held.

holding.description: Whether the report indicates an object is held.

jaw_rad.description: Measured jaw position in motor radians.

live.description:
Whether `jaw_rad` and `torque_nm` are a live reading of the idle motor
(true) or the last stroke's telemetry (false, motor busy or silent).

open_rad.description: Configured open ceiling in motor radians, when published by the backend.

overload_released.description:
Whether the hold behind this report had to be opened PAST the measured
jaws to bring its standing torque under the ceiling.

The grip that is standing is not the grip that was asked for: the hold
stands at zero preload, and `holding` says whether anything is still
between the jaws. A caller carrying an object on the strength of a
`grasp` needs to know the grasp was given up underneath it.

target_closedness.description:
The newest streamed target, as a closedness in `0.0..=1.0`, or `None`
when nothing has been posted to the `target` lane since the last
blocking stroke.

This is what was ASKED for, not where the jaws are; `jaw_rad` is where
they are.

tracking.description:
Whether the `target` lane is driving the jaws toward
`target_closedness` right now.

False once the target has been reached and nothing new was posted, and
false for every gripper driven only by the blocking verbs.

GripperSlot.description:
Either the device's own state or, when that device could not be
read, a [`SlotError`] naming the failure.

oneOf.description: The device answered; this is its state.
The device could not be read.

GripperSlots.description: The two grippers' slots, keyed by side.

allOf.description: How hard to hold an object met on the way.

closedness.description: Fraction of the stroke from open (0) to closed (1).

jaw_rad.description: Absolute jaw position in motor radians.

GripperTarget.description:
A continuous gripper target.

Exactly one of `closedness` and `jaw_rad` is given. `closedness` is the hand-protocol
convention shared with dx-manipulator's wire units: `0.0` is the commanded
open ceiling, `1.0` the closed stop, linear in motor radians between them.
`jaw_rad` addresses the motor directly, in the same radians the stroke
report's `jaw_rad` uses. The backend resolves either to a motor target and
refuses values outside the mechanism's range. The flattened
[`GripRequest`] fields (`grip`, `grip_preload_rad`) say how hard to hold
whatever the stroke meets on the way.

HandCapabilities.description: What one hand can do, so a consumer can negotiate instead of assuming.

axis_names.description: The axis names, in command order.

features.description:
Capability tokens this driver implements. Names, not version numbers:
a token is a promise that something works, tokens are added but never
renamed or removed, and a consumer tests for the one it needs.

max_command_hz.description:
The vendor-rated command rate ceiling in hertz, covering commands AND
polls together.

num_axes.description: How many axes a command carries.

side.description: Which arm side it is mounted on.

wire_max.description: The maximum raw value of [`HandUnit::Wire`] for this model.

axes.description:
One value per axis, in the model's own axis order (which
[`HandCapabilities::axis_names`] publishes). The length must match
[`HandCapabilities::num_axes`].

HandDriveBlocker.description:
One unmet precondition of hand-driving, with the sentence that says what
to do about it.

reason.description: What it means and what clears it, in one sentence.

HandDriveBlockerKind.description:
One precondition of hand-driving the mobile base that is not currently
met.

HandModel.description:
Which dexterous hand is fitted to a side.

The wire spelling is the `"<maker>/<model>"` id the retiring
`omakase_hands` package used, so a configuration or a consumer moving off
that package keeps the same string.

HandSlot.description:
Either the device's own state or, when that device could not be
read, a [`SlotError`] naming the failure.

oneOf.description: The device answered; this is its state.
The device could not be read.

HandState.description: One sampled snapshot of a hand.

all_enabled.description: Whether the daemon believes every axis is enabled.

enabled.description: Per-axis enabled flags, as the hand reports them.

error_code.description:
The most recent device error record: `0` means none. On the O30 this
is the hand-wide MI `0x4F` communication error; on the DH116S it is
the first faulted axis's code.

faults.description: Human descriptions of every fault currently reported.

features.description:
Capability tokens, repeated here so a consumer that only polls state
does not have to fetch capabilities separately.

live.description:
Whether `positions` came from a reading taken for THIS call, rather
than from the last one the command path happened to take.

A read on these hands is not free — it competes with the command path
for the arm's single passthrough channel — so a busy hand answers
with its last sample and says so here, exactly as the gripper's
report does.

positions.description: Per-axis measured position as a fraction of the axis's range.

positions_wire.description: Per-axis measured position in the raw vendor unit.

side.description: Which arm side it is mounted on.

HandUnit.description:
The unit a [`HandCommand`]'s values are in. See the module docs for why
degrees are not among them.

backend.description: The backend the daemon was started with, such as `real` or `sim`.

commit.description:
The source commit the daemon was built from, or `null` when the build
was not told one.

The key is always present: a daemon built without a declared commit
answers `null` rather than omitting the field, so a consumer reading
it can tell "this build does not know" from "this response is from an
older daemon".

uptime_s.description:
Whole seconds since this frontend started serving.

The WebSocket `health` method reports the same field with fractional
seconds.

JointCalibration.description:
Per-joint calibration read from the board's `robot.ini` (the `.BASIC`
section of each joint).

torque_max.description:
Maximum torque (`TorqueMax`, from the joint's `.BASIC` section — not the
separate `.MOTOR` section's rated torque).

position.description: Target angle for that joint in degrees.

wait.description: Block until the arm reports arrival (up to 30 s).

Joints7.description:
Seven arm joint values in SDK order J1 through J7, in degrees unless a
field explicitly documents another unit.

joints_deg.description: Target joint angles in degrees, seven joints.

wait.description:
Block until the arm reports arrival (up to 30 s) rather than
returning as soon as the command is accepted.

KeepOutsPut.description:
`PUT /v1/chassis/maps/{scene}/keep_outs`.

Whole-sub-resource replacement, matching [`RoadPut`]'s semantics: the two
fields are the scene's complete keep-out and typed-zone geometry
afterwards, not a delta, so writing both empty clears the scene. Each
point in `forbidden_areas` and in a [`SpliceAreaPut`]'s `points` accepts
either the base's own `[x, y]` array spelling or the `{"x": x, "y": y}`
object spelling the keep-out `GET` serves inside each
`forbiddenAreasTemp` string (`d1fw_core::Point`), so a caller that echoes
a point it just read back into a write is accepted too.

forbidden_areas.description:
The keep-out geometry: one entry per area, each a list of `[x, y]`
points (exactly two is a virtual wall segment, three or more a
forbidden polygon).

KernelLog.description: A verbatim tail of the board's kernel ring buffer (`dmesg`).

captured_unix_ms.description: Capture time on the firmware host, Unix epoch milliseconds.

lines.description: The kernel log lines, verbatim and in order.

source.description: Where this report came from (e.g. `root@192.168.9.100` or `sim`).

KernelModule.description: One loaded kernel module of interest (from `lsmod`).

size.description: Module size in bytes as reported by `lsmod`.

used_by.description: Names of modules that depend on this one (the `lsmod` "Used by" list).

KillSnapshot.description: A copyable snapshot of every device's soft-kill latch.

LeaseClass.description:
How privileged one lease request is, and therefore what it may displace:
`ambient` (rank 10) < `policy` (50) < `operator` (90).

A request of a strictly higher class than the current holder preempts it;
an equal class is first-come and a lower one is refused. Three named
classes rather than a free integer, because a rank is only useful if two
consumers written by two people mean the same thing by it. The numeric
ranks are published for consumers whose own arbiter works in numbers —
omakase-core's does — but the wire form is always the name.

unlock.description: `true` releases drive motors for manual pushing; `false` engages them.

MapResource.description:
One saved scene, with its waypoints.

The same header fields as [`MapSummary`] plus the waypoint list itself.
The waypoints are forwarded exactly as the mobile base's own interface
produced them and are not reshaped: the shape belongs to the base, and a
caller drawing a map needs every field the base kept, including ones this
crate has no name for.

origin.description: Map origin `[x, y, z]` in the scene's coordinate frame.

resolution.description: Metres per pixel of the scene's map image.

scene.description: The vendor scene name, which is this resource's identifier.

waypoints.description: The scene's waypoints, forwarded unchanged from the base.

MapSummary.description:
One saved scene as the map collection lists it.

The typed summary of a scene: enough to draw a list, place the scene's
image in metres and say how many waypoints it holds, without fetching the
waypoints themselves. Composed from the vendor's scene list, its
per-scene origin and its per-scene waypoint list.

origin.description: Map origin `[x, y, z]` in the scene's coordinate frame.

point_count.description: How many waypoints the scene's road network holds.

resolution.description: Metres per pixel of the scene's map image.

scene.description: The vendor scene name, which is this resource's identifier.

MappingGrid.description: Typed ROS occupancy grid, with x varying fastest and y increasing by row.

cells.description: -1 unknown, 0 free through 100 occupied; exactly width*height cells.

frame_id.description: Received coordinate frame; never assumed map.

origin_orientation.description: Origin quaternion x/y/z/w, validated unit length.

origin_position.description: Origin position x/y/z in received frame.

MappingGridReading.description: One independently aged stream; payload is null when client's revision matches.

age_ms.description: Monotonic age of latest valid receipt.

error.description: Rejection/error detail; never silently replaced with fresh old data.

oneOf.description: Full valid payload when changed; null otherwise. Retain by revision.

received_at_unix_ms.description: Local time of the latest valid receipt.

revision.description: Monotonic local payload revision, retained across reconnects.

MappingJogDelivery.description: Delivery evidence for one HTTP command.

MappingJogDirection.description: One fixed motion axis per hold; no diagonal input.

MappingJogPhase.description: Lifecycle of this daemon's local intent, never a claim about physical stopping.

MappingJogRequest.description: Typed operator action. A renewal never changes direction or resurrects an ended lease.

oneOf.description: Begin one hold after reviewing current scene and control token.

expected_control_token.description: Opaque token from GET state; stop invalidates it even before start arrives.

speed.description: Positive magnitude in metres/sec or radians/sec for the chosen axis.

oneOf.description: Refresh only the identified live lease.

lease_id.description: Exact opaque lease identity from start acknowledgment.

oneOf.description: End local intent and attempt explicit zero, even while killed or stale.

MappingJogState.description: Latest bounded lease and command-delivery state.

admissible.description:
Whether this daemon's standing preconditions for a mapping jog are
met, so that a start is worth attempting at all.

`false` means a start WILL be refused, whatever the operator does at
the console: the configuration or the mobile base's firmware
generation rules it out, and nothing about the jog request can change
that. [`Self::inadmissible_reason`] says which condition failed.

`true` is not a promise that a start succeeds. It means only that
these standing conditions hold; the momentary ones are checked at the
request -- the manufacturer ROS topics must be fresh and consistent
with the named scene, an outstanding [`Self::stop_required`] must be
cleared first, and the lease and the stopping epoch are re-checked
before every send.

angular_max_rad_s.description: Application angular ceiling, not a proven hardware limit.

control_token.description: Opaque current admission revision; changes at stopping intent and daemon restart.

oneOf.description: Fixed direction of current/last hold.

inadmissible_reason.description:
Which standing precondition rules a mapping jog out, or `null` when
[`Self::admissible`] is true.

lease_id.description: Current or last lease identity, absent before first start.

lease_ms.description: Maximum time granted by one renewal.

linear_max_m_s.description: Application linear ceiling, not a proven hardware limit.

motion_delivery.description: Last nonzero delivery, not measured motion.

physical_completion.description: Physical movement and stopping remain unknown.

remaining_ms.description: Remaining local hold time; zero outside active phase.

stop_required.description: Requires an explicit successful zero request before new local intent.

zero_delivery.description: Last explicit zero delivery, not measured stopping.

MappingMapSource.description: Which of the two occupancy-grid readings describes the base's map now.

MappingScan.description: Frame-local laser scan. No map transform is inferred.

ranges.description: Metres; null means invalid/no return, never a zero-distance obstacle.

MappingScanReading.description: One independently aged stream; payload is null when client's revision matches.

age_ms.description: Monotonic age of latest valid receipt.

error.description: Rejection/error detail; never silently replaced with fresh old data.

oneOf.description: Full valid payload when changed; null otherwise. Retain by revision.

received_at_unix_ms.description: Local time of the latest valid receipt.

revision.description: Monotonic local payload revision, retained across reconnects.

MappingStamp.description: ROS source timestamp; distinct from receipt time and not a freshness guarantee.

nsecs.description: Source nanoseconds, less than one billion.

MappingStreamRequest.description: Optional client revisions suppress unchanged payloads, not status metadata.

map_modify_revision.description: Last retained localization-map revision; omit to receive a full frame.

map_revision.description: Last retained map revision; omit to receive a full valid frame.

scan_revision.description: Last retained scan revision; omit to receive a full valid scan.

stream_id.description: Reader instance identity returned previously; mismatches force full payloads.

MappingStreamStatus.description: Receipt validity; fresh receipt does not prove a changing source map.

MappingStreams.description: Separate read-only bridge stream; never issues command or publish messages.

connection.description: This stream connection, independent of control-state ROS reader.

map.description:
Latest `/map` occupancy grid: the SLAM node's live map, mapping only.

Outside mapping mode nothing publishes this topic and the status is
not_published_in_this_mode.

map_modify.description:
Latest `/map_modify` occupancy grid: the loaded scene's map.

The base's decision node publishes this topic latched, once, when it
loads a scene, so one frame arrives on subscription and no further
frame arrives until a scene is loaded again. Receipt age is therefore
the age of the last scene load, and a large age_ms is normal; this
reading goes stale by the same policy as the others and staleness here
does not mean the map changed.

map_source.description: Which reading is authoritative for the base's current mode.

max_map_cells.description: Application cell budget, not a manufacturer maximum.

max_scan_samples.description: Application ray budget, not a manufacturer maximum.

stale_after_ms.description: Receipt freshness threshold; application policy, not vendor guarantee.

stream_id.description: Reader identity, stable across reconnects but different after daemon restart.

Motion.description:
Whether the robot is moving right now, as the whole-robot snapshot
answers it.

This exists for the question "is it safe to stop or restart the daemon
now?". `deploy/systemd/d1-firmwared.service` chooses `KillSignal=SIGKILL`
so the arms hold their pose across a restart, and states the cost of that
choice plainly: a device that is mid-motion is NOT quiesced on stop. An
OTA config plane that wants to restart the unit has to be able to ask the
machine, rather than trusting an operator to remember.

Derived ONLY from motion facts the devices already report — no timer, no
bookkeeping of commands in flight — so it describes the machine and not
the daemon's memory of it:

| source | means moving |
| --- | --- |
| [`crate::ArmState::stationary`] (both sides) | `false` |
| [`crate::SliderState::moving`] | `true` |
| [`crate::ChassisState::navigating`] | `true` |
| [`crate::GripperReport::tracking`] (both sides) | `true` |
| [`crate::NeckState::moving`] | `true` |

Two limits, stated rather than hidden:

- The NECK is answered at the resolution of its own wire. Its motors
  report no "moving" bit, so the backend compares each axis' measured
  velocity against one count of the feedback's twelve-bit velocity field
  (`0.022 rad/s`); a neck commanded slower than that creeps invisibly and
  contributes `false`. That is a property of the DM protocol, not a
  threshold this daemon chose.
- A gripper driven by the BLOCKING verbs is not represented either:
  `tracking` describes the streaming `target` lane only. Such a stroke is
  bounded and is held open by its own in-flight request.

A consumer deciding whether a restart is safe must treat everything that
is not [`Motion::Idle`] as unsafe. [`Motion::Unknown`] is reported when a
device that contributes to the answer could not be read, and must never be
read as "idle": not knowing is not the same as standing still.

MotorState.description:
Whether the mobile base's drive motors are engaged, as far as this daemon
can tell.

The vendor's `lockCtrl` endpoint writes this and NOTHING reads it back:
`getRobotInfo` carries no field for it and the vendor's own web
application never displays one. So this is the daemon's memory of its own
last successful write, and [`ChassisControlState::motors_source`] says
whether there was one.

orient.description: The orientation the chassis should turn to in place.

enabled.description: Start navigation when true; close navigation when false.

NavigationState.description:
The mobile base's autonomous-navigation state, decoded from the vendor's
`autoStatus` field.

The vendor's own dictionary for that field, as its web application's
status page renders it and as the vendor SDK's `monitor/codes.py` spells
it, is `0` navigation not started, `1` localizing, `2` ready/arrived, `3`
moving, `4` path blocked, `5` paused, `6` the goal point is occupied, `7`
localization lost, `8` sensor data lost.

`autoStatus` is a NAVIGATION field, and the base does not clear it when it
leaves navigation mode: a base sitting in the vendor's remote-control mode
can still be reporting the `3` it was reporting when its last trip was
interrupted. Reading it without checking the work mode first is therefore
how a consumer convinces itself a stationary base is driving, so this is
[`Off`](Self::Off) whenever [`ChassisControlState::mode`] is not
[`WorkMode::Navigation`], and the untouched field is still on the wire as
[`ChassisControlState::auto_status_raw`].

A requested slider move: one absolute height, or one small relative
amount.

Exactly one of `height_m` and `delta_m` is given. Neither and both are
both rejected with `400` rather than resolved by a precedence rule: a
caller that sent two targets did not mean one of them, and a caller that
sent none named no move at all.

`delta_m` is the commissioning form. It is admitted only on a daemon
started with `[slider] commissioning = true`, it is capped at
[`crate::safety::SLIDER_COMMISSIONING_STEP_MAX_M`] per call, and it runs
at a fixed low speed — so `speed_ratio` may not be sent with it. It is on
this verb rather than on a new one because on the LD2-RS's wire the two
are the same PR path write with a different mode word (`0x0041` instead
of `0x0001`), so a separate verb would have been a second name for one
operation.

delta_m.description:
A small relative amount in metres, measured from where the carriage
stands now; negative is down. Commissioning only.

height_m.description:
Absolute target height in metres, measured from the drive's origin.

Optional in the schema only because `delta_m` is the alternative; a
body carrying neither is refused.

Optional move speed as a normalized ratio in `0.0..=1.0`: a fraction of
the slider's full speed, the same convention the arm's `vel_ratio`
uses (a fraction of full speed, never a percentage). `None` (the field
absent from the request body) keeps the backend's default speed, so an
existing caller is unchanged. Out-of-range values are rejected with
`400`. It may not be combined with `delta_m`, which always moves at a
fixed low commissioning speed.

wait.description: Wait for the backend to report completion when true.

confirm.description: Must be exactly `SET_LIMITS`. Anything else is a `400`.

lower_m.description:
The lowest height this unit may be commanded to, in metres. Not below
`0`.

upper_m.description:
The highest height this unit may be commanded to, in metres. Not above
the model ceiling `[slider] travel_max_m`: a unit calibration may only
narrow.

confirm.description:
Must be exactly `SET_ZERO`. Anything else is a `400`, and the body is
required: this verb throws away the lift's origin, and an empty POST
is how a console button or a curl retry reaches a route by accident.

read, a [`SlotError`] naming the failure.

The device could not be read.

The raw `Pr0.15` absolute-encoder setting the decision was made from
(`1` = multi-turn absolute enabled, which is the only commissioned
value), or `null` when the drive has not answered a reading of it.

Published because `zero_reference: "unknown"` is otherwise a verdict
with no evidence: this field and `height_m` are the two readings that
produced it.

An INFO-level suggestion about the origin above, when it earns one.

Additive and absent when it does not, so a consumer that has never
heard of it reads exactly the state it always read. A commissioned
and verified lift never carries one. See [`crate::slider_advisory`].

alarm_code.description:
The masked 12-bit raw alarm register value (see
`d1fw_proto_slider::AlarmCode`). `0` when the drive reports no alarm,
and also `0` when `comms_ok` is false since a failed read carries no
trustworthy register content.

comms_ok.description: Whether communications with the slider are healthy.

travel_limits.description:
Every layer that constrains travel, and the range they come to
together — the one `set_height` admits.

Additive to `travel_max_m`, which is unchanged and still the model
ceiling: `travel_limits.model.upper_m` is the same number. A console
that reads only `travel_max_m` keeps working and simply does not know
about a unit calibration narrower than the model.

Like `zero_verification` and `advisory`, this is filled where the
daemon hands the state out ([`crate::D1::slider_state`] and the
`/v1/state` snapshot) rather than by the backend: the unit layer
lives in the daemon's own state file, which no device can read. A
state taken straight from a device therefore carries the model layer
alone.

travel_max_m.description:
The upper bound of the slider's usable travel in metres — the highest
`height_m` a move may target. Sourced from the daemon's `[slider]
travel_max_m` configuration (default `0.30` on a D1) so a console can
present the real limit instead of hardcoding one. The lower bound is
always `0.0` (the homed position), so no separate minimum is
published. Carried even when `comms_ok` is false, since it is a
configured fact rather than a live reading.

Whether the drive's zero is plausibly the commissioned one. `unknown`
means `set_height` and `home` are refused with `409` until the
commissioning procedure has been run — see [`ZeroReference`].

zero_verification.description:
Whether the origin this daemon last wrote has been read back across a
power cycle. See [`ZeroVerification`].

SliderTravelLimits.description:
Every layer that constrains how far the torso lift may travel, and what
they come to together.

The layers exist because "how high can this lift go" has more than one
answer and an operator needs to know WHICH one stopped a move. The model
ceiling is what a D1's lift is; the unit calibration is what this
particular machine's jig, cabling and mechanical build turned out to
allow, measured on a bench and recorded in the daemon's state file.

A layer only ever NARROWS: a unit calibration that claimed more travel
than the model has is refused when it is recorded, so `effective` can
never be wider than `model`.

The intersection of every layer above: the range `set_height`
actually admits.

What the model allows: `[0, travel_max_m]` from `[slider]

UltrasonicChannel.description:
One channel of the mobile base's ultrasonic proximity ring.

The base reports a channel that received no echo, or whose target is
beyond its range, as the sentinel distance `100.0` metres rather than as a
failure. That sentinel is NOT a distance, so [`UltrasonicChannel::range_m`]
is `null` for such a channel and the untouched number stays on
[`UltrasonicChannel::raw_range_m`] where an operator checking the hardware
can still see exactly what the base said.

How long ago this channel's reading was taken, in milliseconds.

`0` means the channel was in the newest frame the daemon read. A
larger value means it was not, and this is still the last thing that
channel said: the base's own example capture shows three channels on a
chassis configured for four, so a channel dropping out of the array is
a thing the service does rather than an error.

The channel's beam width in radians, or `null` when the frame carried
no such field.

The channel's maximum range in metres, or `null` when the frame
carried no such field. This is the bound `valid` is tested against, so
a channel with no bound is never valid.

min_range_m.description:
The channel's minimum range in metres, or `null` when the frame
carried no such field.

A reading below this bound is still reported as valid: on a proximity
sensor that is an object closer than the transducer can measure, which
is the ring's most important answer, not a fault.

reaches a terminal phase.

message.description: Human-readable detail; empty when there is none.

phase.description: The phase the goal has reached.

WsRequest.description: One request frame sent by a WebSocket client.

id.description:
Caller-chosen correlation identifier, echoed in the response.

Responses can arrive out of order (see [`WsResponse`]), so this is the
only way to match a response to its request.

method.description:
The `x-ws-method` value of the operation to call, for example
`arm.a.move_joints`.  Side-templated operations are spelled with a
concrete side: `arm.a.mode`, never `arm.{side}.mode`.

params.description: The operation's request body, as an object.  Omitted means `{}`.

WsResponse.description:
One response frame, carrying the same payload the REST envelope would.

**Responses are not ordered.**  Each request is dispatched on its own
task, so a long motion call never delays another request on the same
connection and a later request can answer first.  Correlate by `id`, never
by arrival order.

code.description:
The mobile base's own numeric response code, when the failure came
from the base. Null on a failure raised by the daemon itself, and
absent from a success frame, which carries the three fields it has
always carried.

The same field the REST failure envelope carries, so a consumer that
speaks both frontends branches on one vocabulary.

data.description:
The operation's result on success, null on error.  This is the same
payload as the REST envelope's `data` for the same method.

id.description:
The `id` of the request this answers, or null when the frame could not
be parsed far enough to recover one.

oneOf.description:
The stable machine word for the failure; absent from a success frame.

Branch on this rather than on `message`, which is the daemon's or the
mobile base's own sentence and is free to change.

message.description: The failure reason on error, null on success.

WsSoftKillEvent.description:
An unsolicited frame pushed when one device's soft-kill latch changes.

It has no `id`: it answers no request.  Distinguish pushes from responses
by the presence of `event`.

killed.description: The device's latch value after the transition.

WsSubscribeParams.description:
The `params` of a `subscribe` request.

A subscription names a read and is answered with that read's value now,
and again whenever the value changes. It is not a second API: the value
pushed is exactly what the named method would have answered.

interval_ms.description:
How often to sample, in milliseconds.

Clamped server-side to the method's floor and reported back in
[`WsSubscribeResult::interval_ms`]; a value below the floor is clamped,
not refused. `state` and every other read default to 500 ms with a
floor of 200 ms, because one `state` read costs an HTTP round trip to
the mobile base plus a serial and a Modbus round trip on the robot.
`arm.a.state` and `arm.b.state` default to 100 ms with a floor of
50 ms: they are answered from the arm feedback stream and touch no bus.

method.description:
The read to subscribe to, spelled as an `x-ws-method` value with a
concrete side: `state`, `arm.a.state`, `chassis.state`.

Only operations whose HTTP verb is `GET` can be subscribed to, and
only those this frontend dispatches: a method that writes, or one
marked REST-only, is refused.

params.description:
The parameters that read takes, if any. Forwarded unchanged to every
sample. Omitted means `{}`.

interval_ms.description: The sampling interval actually in force, after clamping.

method.description: The method that was subscribed to, echoed.

subscription.description:
The identifier every [`WsUpdateEvent`] of this subscription carries,
and the one to pass to `unsubscribe`.

Per-connection and starting at 1: it means nothing on another
connection, and a reconnecting client counts from 1 again.

The identifier the matching `subscribe` answered with. An identifier
that is not live on this connection is a `not_found` error.

WsUpdateEvent.description:
One sample of a subscription, pushed by the server.

The first one follows the `subscribe` response immediately. After that a
frame is sent only when the value CHANGES: consecutive identical samples
are dropped, so silence means the reading has not moved. There is no
heartbeat, because the connection itself carries WebSocket ping/pong and
its liveness is observable there.

A sample whose read FAILED is pushed like any other, with `data` null and
the failure in `message`/`code`/`kind`, and the subscription stays alive:
a device that is unreachable for one sample is expected to come back, and
the consumer would otherwise have to resubscribe to find out that it did.

code.description:
The mobile base's own numeric response code when the failure came from
the base, null otherwise.

data.description: The value the method answered with, or null when the read failed.

oneOf.description:
The stable machine word for the failure, null when the sample
succeeded. Branch on this to tell a failed sample from a successful
one, rather than on `data` being null.

message.description: The failure reason when the read failed, null otherwise.

method.description: The method being sampled, echoed from the subscription.

subscription.description: The subscription this sample belongs to.

ZeroReference.description:
Whether the torso lift's drive origin is the one it was commissioned with.

The LD2-RS keeps its zero in the absolute encoder, and every height this
daemon accepts is measured from it. A drive that has lost that zero — a new
drive, an EEPROM that did not survive, a swapped motor — still answers
every register read: it simply calls some other place "0 m". A move to 0 m
against such an origin drives the lift into its mechanical stop.

So the origin is a published fact rather than an assumption, decided from
two readings the drive itself supplies: `Pr0.15` (the absolute-encoder
setting, which must be "multi-turn absolute enabled") and the current
position, which on a commissioned drive has to lie inside the usable
travel. See `d1fw_backends::slider::zero_reference`.

ZeroVerification.description:
Whether a zero that was written has been proved to have survived a power
cycle.

Separate from [`ZeroReference`] on purpose, and additive to it: the two
answer different questions and a consumer that only knows the older one
keeps reading exactly what it read. `zero_reference` asks "can the drive
vouch for its origin right now", which is decided from live readings.
This asks "has the origin this daemon last wrote been read back after the
power was removed", which no live reading can answer — it is a fact about
history, so it lives in the daemon's state file.

It matters because the LD2-RS reports its EEPROM save as taken (`0x5555`)
before anything has proved the parameter is still there after power is
removed, and an origin that lived in RAM only is precisely the failure
`set_zero` exists to prevent.

info.description:
The `d1-firmwared` HTTP API: one guarded surface over the D1's arms, grippers, pan/tilt neck, eye LED controller, vertical slider and mobile chassis.

## This API is unauthenticated

The daemon performs **no authentication and no authorization of any kind**. Every caller that can open the port can move a 110 kg robot. It binds the loopback interface by default; keep it there. To reach it from another host, tunnel it over SSH or an equivalently authenticated channel — do not bind it to a routable address and do not put it behind a bare reverse proxy. The `security: []` below is a statement of fact, not an omission.

## Ratios are fractions, not percentages

Every `vel_ratio` and `acc_ratio` field is a **fraction of full speed in `0.0..=1.0`**. `0.1` means 10% of full speed. `100` does not mean 100%: it is out of range and is rejected with a 400. This has caused a real full-speed-arm incident on a robot, which is why the value is now refused rather than clamped.

## Every response is enveloped

Three operations are exceptions on success. `GET /v1/chassis/maps/{scene}/image` returns raw `image/png`, `GET /v1/recorder/dumps/{id}/files/{name}` returns one window of a dump's file as that file's own bytes (`application/x-ndjson` or `application/json`, with `X-Dump-File-Offset`, `X-Dump-File-Total-Bytes` and `X-Dump-File-Eof` saying where the window sits), and `GET /v1/chassis/ultrasonic/stream` returns a `text/event-stream` whose events carry a bare reading rather than an envelope. All three still answer failures with the error envelope, so branch on the response content type and not on the status alone. Otherwise every response body is `{"status", "data", "message"}`. `status` is `ok` or `error`; `message` is always present and is `null` on success; `data` is `null` for commands that return nothing, and `null` on every error. Unknown routes and unknown methods answer with the same 404 envelope rather than a framework 404 or 405.

## Operator arbitration: the arm lease

Several consumers can reach this daemon at once, so the arms carry an optional **lease**: `POST /v1/arm/lease` `{"holder", "ttl_s", "class"}` takes, renews or preempts it, `DELETE /v1/arm/lease` `{"holder"}` hands it back, and `GET /v1/arm/lease` (also `arm.lease` in `/v1/state`) says who holds it. While it is held, the operations marked `x-arm-lease` refuse anyone else with **409** and a message naming the holder and its class; those operations accept a `holder` field in their request body, which is how the holder identifies itself. Everything else — every read, `soft_kill`, `release_soft_kill`, `estop`, `clear_errors` and `recover` — is never arbitrated: the verbs that stop a robot or bring it back must not be withholdable by an operator who has walked away.

**Priority.** A lease is taken in one of three classes — `ambient` (rank 10), `policy` (50), `operator` (90) — and a strictly higher class takes the arms off a lower one: a person at a teleop station or the console outranks a policy, which outranks the robot's ambient motion. Equal classes are first-come. **A request that names no class is `ambient`**, the lowest privilege, so consumers can be taught their class one release at a time. A preemption cancels the displaced holder's trajectory and waits — at most 250 ms — for its commands to finish before the grant is recorded, and is refused rather than granted if the arms will not go quiet. Nothing is pushed to the displaced holder: it learns from `epoch`/`holder` changing on `GET /v1/arm/lease`, or from its next gated POST answering 409.

It is **opt-in and lazily expiring**: with no lease held every verb behaves exactly as it did before, and a lease whose TTL has run out is simply taken by the next caller. The holder and its class are self-declared, not credentials — see the authentication note above. The WebSocket frontend carries no holder in its frames and is therefore not arbitrated.

## Blocking calls

Several operations block for real robot motion. Each carries an `x-timeout-seconds` extension giving the longest it is expected to take, so a generated client can size its own timeout: the slider's `set_height` with `wait: true` can take five minutes, gripper strokes about 40 seconds, arm recovery about 65 seconds, and a waited joint move about 30 seconds. A client default of a few seconds will time out on a call that is working correctly.

## The same verbs over WebSocket

The WebSocket frontend (default `ws://127.0.0.1:4751/v1/ws`) speaks the same verbs over one persistent connection. An operation callable that way carries an `x-ws-method` extension naming the method to put in a `WsRequest`; an operation without one is REST-only. Requests are dispatched concurrently, so **responses can arrive out of order** — correlate them by `id`, never by arrival order. The connection also pushes unsolicited `WsSoftKillEvent` and `WsNavEvent` frames, told apart from responses by their `event` field.

**A read-only copy on this origin.** The same protocol is served at `/v1/ws` on the REST origin as well, so a page served from it — the web console at `/ui/` — can hold one connection without knowing the WebSocket listener's port. That copy dispatches ONLY the operations whose verb is `GET` plus the subscription vocabulary below; anything that writes is refused there with `kind: not_found` and a message naming the port that offers it. The reason is arbitration: WebSocket frames carry no lease `holder`, so motion over this protocol is unarbitrated, and an unarbitrated motion lane does not belong on the origin the console is served from.

**That copy checks `Origin`.** A browser applies the same-origin policy to the REST `GET` routes and applies none of it to a WebSocket upgrade, so the route does the equivalent itself, before upgrading: an upgrade carrying no `Origin` is accepted (every non-browser client sends none), as is one whose `Origin` is the origin it was sent to — `http://` or `https://` plus the request's own `Host` — or one listed in the daemon's `[rest] cors_allow_origins`, matched exactly as the CORS allow-list is. Anything else is refused with **403** and `kind: refused`, and no connection is opened. The WebSocket listener on its own port takes no such check.

**Subscriptions.** Two methods are this protocol's own and are in no operation's `x-ws-method`, because they have no REST route: `subscribe` (`WsSubscribeParams` → `WsSubscribeResult`) turns any subscribable `GET` method into a server push, and `unsubscribe` (`WsUnsubscribeParams` → `WsUnsubscribeResult`) stops one. The samples arrive as `WsUpdateEvent` frames: the first immediately, then only when the value changes. Sampling intervals are clamped to a per-method floor and the effective one is reported; one connection may hold 32 subscriptions, and all of them end when it closes.

## Clients are generated, not shipped

This document is the deliverable. See the repository README for the exact commands for `openapi-python-client`, `openapi-typescript` + `openapi-fetch`, and `progenitor`.

post.description:
Arbitration between the consumers that can all reach this daemon — a teleop session, a policy, and the robot's own ambient motion. While a lease is held, arm motion from anyone else is refused with 409 naming the holder; reads, `estop`, `clear_errors`, `recover` and the soft kill are never arbitrated.

Granted when the lease is free, when the current one has expired, or when you already hold it — that last case is the heartbeat, so renew by repeating this call well inside `ttl_s`. `ttl_s` defaults to 30 seconds and may not exceed 600; expiry is evaluated when the lease is next read, so a consumer that dies frees the arms without anything having to notice it died.

**Priority.** `class` is `ambient` (rank 10), `policy` (50) or `operator` (90), and **an omitted `class` means `ambient`** — the lowest privilege there is, so a consumer written before classes existed cannot outrank one written after. A request of a strictly HIGHER class than the holder preempts it: the answer carries `preempted_from` and a new `epoch`. An equal class is first-come (409), and a lower one is 409 too. `epoch` increments on every fresh grant and never on a heartbeat, so a consumer that reads its own name back can tell "I still hold these" from "I lost them and have them again" — and therefore whether what it believed about the arms is stale.

**A preemption stops the arms first.** The displaced holder's trajectory is cancelled (`cancelled`, not `failed`) and both arms are taken exclusively before the grant is recorded, so the new holder never inherits a moving robot. The arm mode is deliberately NOT changed: a position or torque hold is where the arms are left. If the displaced holder has a command still in flight — a waited `move_joints` is the one that lasts — the hand-over gives up after 250 ms and the preemption is refused with 409 `hand-over timed out; the current holder has a command in flight`; the lease does not move. Stop the robot (`/v1/soft_kill`, `estop` — never leased) and ask again.

There is no push notification: a displaced holder finds out by reading `GET /v1/arm/lease` (different `holder`, different `epoch`) or by having its next gated POST refused.

The holder and the class are self-declared, not credentials: this daemon authenticates nobody, and the lease coordinates cooperating consumers rather than defending against a hostile one. Arbitration is opt-in — with no lease held every verb behaves exactly as it did before.

The servos are off, so **nothing holds the arm: it falls under gravity the instant the brakes open unless somebody is supporting it.**

The body must carry `{"confirm": "RELEASE_BRAKE"}` (otherwise `400`). Accepted only while the arm's servos are off — mode `idle` or `error`; any other mode is a `409` naming the call that idles it. The release is TIMED: `seconds` (`1..=120`, default `30`) after it lands the daemon engages the brakes itself. Sending it again while released restarts the window. The brakes are also engaged by `/v1/arm/{side}/brake_engage`, by `/v1/arm/{side}/estop`, and by the soft kill (which the daemon also runs on shutdown). While released, `mode`, `recover` and a trajectory are refused on this arm, `ArmState` carries `brakes_released: true` and preflight lists it as blocking.

get.description: The same object `GET /v1/chassis/state` carries in its `charge` field, on its own, so an operator interface can follow the charging flow at 1 Hz without pulling the whole chassis reading. Four facts that routinely disagree travel as four fields rather than as one flag: `dock` is where the base is in its docking routine, `auto_charging` is whether automatic charging is the mode it is in, `pack`/`charging`/`basis` are what the battery packs say about current, and `dock_point` is which waypoint pressing charge would send it to. `charging` is null rather than false whenever nothing measured says the base is not charging. Not gated by the chassis soft-kill latch.
get.summary: Read the mobile base's charging state

post.description: Sends the base to the charging dock configured with `chassis_maps_charging_dock_put`, and answers with the charge state read immediately afterwards, so a display starts from a reading rather than from an assumption. It does NOT wait for the base to dock: the base then moves its own fields on its own schedule -- `work_mode` to `auto_charging` and `charge.dock` from `not_docking` to `docking`, then to `docked` once it is on the pile, and finally to `leaving` and back to `not_docking` when it drives off. Whether current is actually flowing is a SEPARATE fact reported only by the battery packs, as `charge.charging` with `charge.basis` saying where that came from; a base can be `docked` with `charging` still null. get.description: The mobile base has exactly ONE control mode at a time and enforces it by IGNORING commands: outside its remote-control mode (`workMode` 4) it answers a jog or a velocity command with HTTP 200 and does not move. This is that mode, decoded, with the control preconditions for sending motion commands, so an operator interface can poll one object at 1 Hz instead of inferring the answer from a digit. The vendor's five modes are its own: `idle` (0, navigation closed), `navigation` (1), `auto_charging` (2), `mapping` (3), `remote_control` (4). `navigation` is the vendor's `autoStatus` decoded, and is `off` in every mode but 1, because the base does NOT clear that field when it leaves navigation -- a stale `moving` read in remote-control mode is the trap this closes; the untouched value is in `auto_status_raw`. `can_hand_drive` is the one-field answer to "do control preconditions permit sending a jog": true only in remote control, not reported in standby, with the emergency switch released and the motors not released by this daemon, and `hand_drive_blockers` names each failing precondition with the sentence that clears it. Unknown motor and standby states do not block. This is permission to send before the separate software stop gate, not proof of physical movement: motor command memory can be stale and the base's bumper interlock can stop motion without blocking transmission. `motors` is NOT a reading from the base: the vendor's `lockCtrl` endpoint writes the motor lock and nothing reads it back, so it is this daemon's record of its own last successful write and `motors_source` is `unknown` until there has been one. `transitions` lists every control verb with whether it is legal from this state and why not -- it describes the MOBILE BASE's mode machine only, and this daemon's chassis soft-kill latch can still refuse an allowed verb with the `kill_latched` kind. get.description: A HARDWARE-CHECK reading: the daemon does not brake, stop or re-route the base on it and it is NOT a safety interlock. The ring is carried only by the vendor's TCP sensor push service, which one mobile-base firmware generation serves and the other does not, so `supported` false with a stated `reason` is a normal answer about the base rather than an error. `supported` true with `source` `none` is the other case: this base does serve the ring, and this read did not get one -- `reason` says why. A channel that received no echo is reported with `valid` false and `range_m` null. The vendor's rule for that is ONE test, `range >= max_range`, and the out-of-range number itself is not a second fact: the D1 mobile base measured on 2026-09-19 sends 65.533 on three channels and 100.0 on a fourth against a `max_range` of 4.5, and both fail the one test. The number stays visible on `raw_range_m`, must never be read as a distance, and must not be used to sort channels into kinds. `age_ms` is per channel as well as per reading, because the base does not always send every configured channel. `link` says how the daemon is currently reading the base: `cycle` for a short connection per read, `held` while a consumer of the stream operation keeps it open.

get.description: The same reading as `GET /v1/chassis/ultrasonic`, pushed as it changes instead of answered once. The response is a `text/event-stream` that stays open until the consumer closes it; each event's `data:` is one complete `ChassisUltrasonic` object, sent bare rather than inside the JSON envelope. An event named `error` carries a plain message string and the stream continues. Events arrive at up to 10 Hz -- a deliberate thinning of the base's own roughly 30 Hz push, sized for a person watching a number move -- and an unchanging reading repeats about once a second so that a still stream and a stalled one are distinguishable. HOLDING THIS OPEN HAS A COST: the ring reaches the daemon over a vendor service that serves ONE client at a time, and for as long as this response is open the daemon holds that slot, so the base's other clients -- the vendor's own diagnostics included -- cannot read it. Close the stream when nothing is watching. `link` reports which shape is in force and, after the held connection ends, when the daemon will try again. Still a HARDWARE-CHECK reading: nothing brakes, stops or re-routes the base on it. Not available over WebSocket.

post.description:
Move the torso lift to 0 m of the current origin (an absolute move, not the drive's homing routine). It is exactly `slider/set_height` with `height_m` 0 and the default speed, and like an unwaited move it returns as soon as the drive has accepted the target — poll `GET /v1/slider/state` for arrival.

This verb does NOT re-reference the drive. Homing, which seeks the mechanical stop and re-zeroes the position counter there, moves whatever origin the robot was commissioned with. That procedure is `slider/set_zero`, which is gated off by default and is not reachable from this verb.

Refused with `409` while `slider/state` reports `zero_reference: "unknown"` — a move to 0 m of an origin the drive cannot vouch for is exactly how the lift reaches its mechanical stop. It is refused the same way when a recorded unit calibration puts its lower bound above 0 m: on such a robot there is no 0 m to go to, and the refusal names that layer.

post.description:
Exactly one of `height_m` and `delta_m` is sent; neither and both are `400`.

`height_m` is metres above the drive's origin. With `wait: true` the call blocks until the slider reports arrival, which is the slowest call in this API; size the client timeout accordingly. It is refused with `409` while `slider/state` reports `zero_reference: "unknown"`: the height is measured from the drive's origin, and a drive that cannot vouch for its origin would take this move somewhere other than where it names. The refusal carries an `advisory` naming the way out. It is refused with `400` when it falls outside the effective range in `slider/state.travel_limits`, and the message names WHICH layer refused it -- the model ceiling `[slider] travel_max_m`, or this unit's recorded calibration.

`delta_m` is a small RELATIVE amount in metres from wherever the carriage stands, negative for down. It depends on no origin, so it is the one move a lift with `zero_reference: "unknown"` can be given -- which is how a carriage is walked down onto its mechanical stop before `slider/set_zero`. It is admitted only on a daemon started with `[slider] commissioning = true` (otherwise `409` with an `advisory`), capped at 0.01 m per call (`400` above that, never silently clamped), and always runs at a fixed low speed, so sending `speed_ratio` with it is a `400` rather than a value quietly ignored. The slider soft-kill latch and `slider/stop` apply to it exactly as to any move.
post.summary: Move the torso lift to an absolute height, or by one small commissioning step

post.description:
**Not a motion verb and not a configuration edit.** Nothing is written to the drive and nothing moves; what is written is the daemon's own state file, and what it decides is the range every later `set_height` is admitted against. It is the unit layer of `slider/state.travel_limits`: what one machine's jig, cabling and mechanical build turned out to allow, measured on a bench once per robot.

A layer may only NARROW. `lower_m` below `0`, or `upper_m` above the model ceiling `[slider] travel_max_m`, is a `400` — a calibration that claimed more travel than the model has would be a calibration that widened it.

Two gates, both required, and the same two `slider/set_zero` has. The daemon must have been started with `[slider] commissioning = true` (otherwise `409`, before the body is parsed), and the body must carry `{"confirm": "SET_LIMITS"}` (otherwise `400`). The slider's soft-kill latch applies.

The record survives a restart: it is in `/var/lib/d1-firmwared/slider.toml`, or wherever `[slider] state_file` points. A daemon that keeps no state file answers `503` rather than accepting a fact it would forget. The response is the state read back, so the new effective range needs no second call.
post.summary: COMMISSIONING ONLY: record how far THIS robot's lift may travel

post.description:
**This is not a motion verb and does not belong on an operator console.** It throws the drive's current zero away and makes the carriage's present position the new 0 m, so every height anything was calibrated against moves with it. Perform it with the lift parked on the mechanical bottom plus 3-4 mm, once, when the drive has no usable zero — a new drive, a replaced motor, an EEPROM that did not survive — which is the state `slider/state` reports as `zero_reference: "unknown"` and which makes `set_height` and `home` answer `409`.

On the wire it is the LD2-RS commissioning sequence: `Pr0.15 = 9` (clear the absolute encoder's multi-turn count, after which the drive restores the parameter to `1` itself), PR trigger `0x0021` (clear the in-RAM position counter), then `0x1801 = 0x2211` (save parameters) polled at `0x1901` until `0x5555`. A save that reports `0xAAAA` is a `502`: the origin would live in RAM only and be gone at the next power cycle.

Two gates, both required. The daemon must have been started with `[slider] commissioning = true` (otherwise `409`, with nothing sent to the drive), and the body must carry `{"confirm": "SET_ZERO"}` (otherwise `400`). The slider's soft-kill latch applies, and a lift that is moving is refused. Afterwards, power-cycle the robot and check `slider/state` again. That step is now mechanical: a successful `set_zero` records the new origin as `zero_verification: "pending"` in the daemon's state file, and the next start promotes it to `"verified"` by itself when the height still reads what it read here. Leave the carriage where `set_zero` left it until that power cycle; a lift that was moved in between reads something else and stays `pending`, which one more power cycle clears. An origin that did not persist is the failure this verb exists to prevent, and `pending` is the daemon saying so out loud.
post.summary: COMMISSIONING ONLY: rewrite the torso lift's origin to where it stands now

get.description:
A direct read of the slider controller over its serial link (about 100-200 ms). An unreadable slider is an error envelope (`502`), unlike the `/v1/state` slot which degrades in place.

`travel_limits` publishes every layer that constrains travel and the `effective` range they come to together, which is the range `set_height` admits: `model` is `[0, travel_max_m]` from the daemon's configuration, and `unit` is this robot's bench calibration or `null` when none has been recorded. A layer only ever narrows.

`zero_verification` is separate from `zero_reference` and additive to it. `zero_reference` asks whether the drive can vouch for its origin right now; this asks whether the origin this daemon last wrote has been read back after a power cycle, which is the only evidence that the drive persisted it rather than holding it in RAM. `unrecorded` means this daemon has no record of setting one and is not a fault.

`advisory` is additive and absent unless the origin earns one; a commissioned and verified lift never carries one. Nothing on the advisory path writes to the drive.

post.summary: Stop slider travel where it is

post.description: The COMPLETE emergency stop of everything this daemon owns, in one call: both arms, both grippers, both hands, the neck, the eyes, the slider and the chassis (zero velocity, navigation paused, light strip off). Do not implement a device-by-device kill above this route. Every latch is set before any stop is issued and the stops run concurrently, so one wedged device cannot delay another; the response reports each action as `ok`, `failed`, `timeout` or `unavailable`, with the milliseconds it took. The chassis actions are bounded at 1 s each and are skipped without any network I/O when the base is known to be absent, so this call returns promptly even against a wedged or missing base. The latch is sticky: motion verbs are refused with 409 until `/v1/release_soft_kill`. This is not a substitute for the physical emergency stop.
